strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear application to embodied AI; identifies underexplored high-density tabletop scene generation
Strong experimental results: collision rates near zero (0.42% vs 8-17% for baselines), 83% user preference over best baseline
Novel two-stage pose and scale alignment approach (DRO + TSA) that effectively decomposes complex spatial reasoning
Comprehensive multi-faceted evaluation: quantitative metrics (LPIPS, DINOv2, CLIP), GPT-4o assessment, large-scale user study (128 participants), and ablation studies
Thorough system integration combining segmentation, completion, 3D generation, and physics-aware assembly into a coherent pipeline
Demonstrates practical applicability with successful robotic manipulation tasks in simulation
Honest presentation including transparent discussion of metric limitations (Fig. 15) and clear stage-wise documentation with intermediate outputs
Good generalization: works on real-world images and stylized inputs; extensive supplementary material with prompts and implementation details
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (GroundedSAM-v2, image-to-3D diffusion, differentiable rendering); DRO and TSA, while practical, represent straightforward applications rather than fundamental innovations

Critical dependency on external proprietary APIs (ChatGPT, Seedream, Hunyuan3D-3.0): limits reproducibility, introduces cost barriers, results may degrade with model updates; 'training-free' claim is misleading
Computational efficiency problematic: 32 minutes per 9-instance scene; sequential execution despite parallelization claims makes large-scale dataset generation impractical for embodied AI
Restricted scope to tabletop scenes with limited evidence of generalization; qualitative-only comparison with most relevant baseline (MesaTask)
Modest test set (78 samples) without statistical significance testing; missing systematic error analysis of failure modes and problematic object categories
Hyperparameter choices (λs, λe, λa, τ) lack justification and sensitivity analysis; RMA-Score's aspect-ratio assumption may fail for certain geometries
Incomplete evaluation of practical utility: sim-to-real transfer quality not thoroughly assessed despite being critical for real-world deployment
Reliance on assumption that top-view provides reliable scale—transparent objects, extreme occlusions, and complex geometries underexplored; occlusion handling may fail in high-density scenarios

strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation with clear criteria for simulation-ready tabletop scenes; identifies genuine gap in existing methods for high-density, collision-free layouts
Exceptionally strong empirical results: near-zero collision rates (0.42% vs 8-17% for baselines), 83.13% user preference with 128 participants, consistent improvements across visual quality metrics
Novel two-stage pose and scale alignment approach (DRO + TSA) effectively decouples complex 3D reasoning; RMA-Score anchor selection is clever and well-motivated

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: multiple evaluation dimensions, large user study with randomized controls, thorough ablations demonstrating necessity of components, comparison with relevant baselines
Pragmatic system design using existing models (ChatGPT, Seedream, Hunyuan3D) enables immediate deployment without retraining; training-free approach is practical
Excellent presentation and reproducibility efforts: detailed supplementary materials with stage-wise intermediate outputs, complete prompts, efficiency analysis, promised code release
Practical utility demonstrated through real-world image reconstruction, scene editing, and robotic manipulation task execution in physics simulation
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily a system combining existing models (GroundedSAM-v2, Hunyuan3D, ChatGPT); DRO is standard differentiable rendering with tri-modal loss; TSA relies on MLLM predictions and handcrafted heuristics rather than principled geometric reasoning

Heavy dependency on proprietary external models (ChatGPT API, Seedream, Hunyuan3D) creates reproducibility concerns; no error analysis for MLLM failures, no fallback mechanisms, error propagation through pipeline not analyzed
Efficiency concerns underexplored: 32 minutes per 9-object scene limits practical deployment; sequential processing despite parallelization potential; scalability to larger scenes unclear

Evaluation methodology has inherent biases: 'best-view' selection favors physically plausible methods (acknowledged by authors in supplementary); test set relatively small (78 samples); LPIPS/DINOv2/CLIP metrics don't directly measure physical plausibility

Limited generalization analysis: tested primarily on standard rectangular tables; only ~2 real-world examples shown; no systematic evaluation of robustness to non-standard geometries, circular/triangular tables, or multi-level surfaces; assumption that vertical axis = 'up' may not generalize

Insufficient ablation studies: individual loss terms (Lsil, Ledge, Lapp) not ablated; loss weights (λs=0.5, λe=0.5, λa=2.0) appear arbitrary without sensitivity analysis; sequential optimization of rotation vs. translation lacks theoretical justification

MLLM reliability not quantified: camera pose accuracy, commonsense size estimation error, and stacking order determination failures not analyzed; multiple failure points in pipeline but no systematic error analysis or reported failure rates

Design choices lack justification: RMA-Score tolerance τ=0.25 selection unexplained; why commonsense size estimation is robust for scale resolution not clearly argued; what happens when MLLM predictions severely fail (e.g., table size overestimation)

Limited comparison scope: only 4 main baselines; text-to-3D comparison (MesaTask) only qualitative; no comparison with simple baselines or other recent embodied AI scene generation work; no analysis of robustness to different image-to-3D models or MLLM choices

Missing failure case analysis: unclear when RMA-Score selection fails, how performance degrades with scene complexity, robustness to highly occluded inputs; limited discussion of method limitations beyond deferred 'future work'

strengths: Addresses a genuine and important bottleneck in robotic manipulation—automated synthesis of large-scale, diverse, physically plausible data
Comprehensive experimental validation including quantitative metrics, large-scale user study (128 participants, 83.13% preference), ablations, and zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on real robot
Strong empirical results: near-zero mesh-level collisions (0.42% vs. 17.39% for MIDI), superior visual metrics (DINOv2: 0.8383 vs. 0.7070), and practical scene editability
Well-motivated technical design: decoupled DRO/TSA approach is sensible; tri-modal loss and RMA-Score are domain-informed
Exceptional reproducibility: detailed supplementary materials with stage-wise outputs, all prompts, experimental protocols, and video demonstrations
Practical system with in-scene editing and direct applicability to physics simulation and policy learning; real robot experiments validate utility
Thorough ablation studies confirm necessity of both DRO and TSA components; comparisons against diverse baselines (ACDC, Gen3DSR, MIDI, MesaTask, Holodeck)
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: DRO applies standard differentiable rendering with existing loss functions; TSA is straightforward geometric computation with heuristics; primary contribution is system integration rather than fundamental innovation

Heavy dependence on black-box LLMs and generative models (ChatGPT, Seedream, Hunyuan3D) raises reproducibility concerns; performance will evolve or degrade as these models change; no sensitivity analysis to model choice
Narrow scope to tabletop environments; generalization to multi-level layouts, shelves, or non-table support structures unexplored; limits broader applicability

Incomplete data-engine validation: lacks large-scale training experiments showing policies trained on synthetic data outperform alternatives; demonstrates only 3 tasks and trajectory synthesis without proving downstream improvements at scale
Modest real-world validation: single robot platform (AgileX PiPER), three manipulation tasks, non-trivial sim-to-real gap (68–84% real vs. 90–98% simulated), only 2,000 trajectories per task

Best-view protocol can mask physically implausible layouts (acknowledged in supplement but main paper relies on it); test set modest (78 scenes, only 4 real photos); GPT-4o evaluation is subjective with known biases

Hyperparameter choices lack justification (e.g., τ=0.25 for RMA-Score, loss weights); MLLM used heuristically across pipeline without error propagation analysis; missing per-component ablations (DRO loss terms)

Missing critical analyses: no computational cost/runtime, failure mode documentation, or guidance on prompt engineering; handling of transparent/reflective/articulated objects not addressed; scene assembly physics details sparse
Comparison fairness concerns: different baselines optimize for different objectives; MesaTask (most comparable) discussed only briefly; some baselines may not represent best-case performance
Limitations section brief and placed at end; does not adequately discuss when method fails, data requirements for effective policy learning, or long-term reproducibility given model dependencies
